message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/parts-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/parts-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:door`, `type:beam`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type` (named `Family: Type`), `family-parameter` (named `Family: Parameter`), …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `level_above`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`, e.g. `types.door`, `types.runs.beam`), `family` (name and definition in `families`), `family_type`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator — another sub-agent), `slabs::view` (floors, ceilings, roofs, shafts, masses — another), `parts::view` (YOURS), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views… — another), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, families, components, stairs… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/parts-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"door"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: PARTS — `src/readers/parts/` (`parts::view` for door, window, component, column, structuralcolumn, footing, beam, stripfooting, pipe, duct, conduit, cabletray, wire, downconductor, groundconductor, cable, rebar, stair, ramp, railing)
Every field `elements` shows for these categories, exactly, for every kind of project. Observed so far (see `big1.bimcraft` and `sample.bimcraft`; verify everything and complete):
- door/window of a project type: `at` (the point on the host wall's location line at `offset` from its start — check arc walls, flipped walls, walls with other location lines), `width`, `height` (the type's), `level` (the host's), `type` (the type's name) and `type_guid`, `sill`, `mark`, flips. Of a family (`family` GUID, `type` a `family-type` GUID): `family` (its name), `family_guid`, `type` (the family type's name, `900 x 2100`; check whether there's a `type_guid`), `operation` (the family's: swing, double-swing, …), `values` (every family parameter worked out for this element: the type's values over the parameters' defaults, formulas evaluated, material parameters as the material's name, plus `Wall Thickness` — the host's thickness), `width`/`height` from `Width`/`Height`. Families loaded with `family` (custom parameters, formulas, instance parameters, yes/no, angles, materials; door/window families with `Sill Height`).
- component: `family`, `family_guid`, `type`, `values` (instance `params` over the type's over the defaults), `height` (find how: the family's forms' top? its `Height`?), `connectors` for electrical families (see the catalog's `family` entry: connectors with `load_va` formulas, poles, voltage, power factor, classification), mirrored, offset, angle, components on upper levels, symbol-only families (`symbol_set`), hosted components if any.
- The family formula language (the catalog's `family` entry): `+ - * / ^`, comparisons `< > = <= >=`, `if`, `and`, `or`, `not`, `min`, `max`, `abs`, `sqrt`, `round`, `roundup`, `rounddown`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan` (degrees), parameter names with spaces, lengths in mm; yes/no parameters; how values print (floats, materials by name, yes/no as booleans?, angles), errors in formulas (what a view shows then). Make it a reusable module with `pub fn family_values(cx: &Ctx, element_id: u64) -> Option<crate::json::Map>` (the `values` of a door/window/component) — the schedule reader will use it for family parameter fields.
- column/structuralcolumn: `type`, `type_guid`, `width`, `depth`, `round` (the type's), `height` (to `top_level` or as stored), `room_bounding` (default true), `base_offset`, `angle`, `top_level`. footing: `height` (its thickness), `base_offset` (−thickness when its top is at the level), `width`/`depth`/`round`.
- beam/stripfooting/pipe/duct/conduit/cabletray/wire/downconductor/groundconductor/cable (runs): `type`, `type_guid`, `width`, `depth`, `round` (the type's), `length` (3D), `axis` (3D end points from the level's elevation, `offset`/`end_offset`, `justify` (top/centre/bottom) and the depth: a 500 deep beam on Level 2 (3000) justified top shows axis z 2750 — the centre line?), `justify`'s default, `system`, risers (start = end with `end_offset`), sloped beams, `closed` chains.
- rebar: `length`, `weight_kg` (steel at 7850 kg/m³: Ø10 × 1000 mm = 0.617), `path` (3D, z over the level), hosted rebar (`host`), `count`/`step` sets, closed hoops, bars made by `reinforce`.
- stair: `end`, `length`, `riser_height` (176.47 = 3000/17 rounded), `risers`, `runs` ([[start, end], …] per run), `height`, `top_level`, landings and turns (`landings: [{at, turn}]`), angle, railings made with it (`railings: true`).
- ramp: `end`, `length`, `runs`, `slope`, landings.
- railing: `type`, `type_guid`, `height` (the type's), `path`; railings hosted on a stair or ramp (`railing {host, side}` or `stair {..., railings: true}`): the path the original works out along its sides (50 mm in from the edges, climbing with it), `base_offset`.
Prioritise what typical scripts make (doors/windows of types and the default families, the default furniture/plumbing/lighting families, columns, beams, pipes, straight stairs, ramps, railings) before exotic cases, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/parts/`.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

content.content:
9 | Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |

14 | Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |

16 | Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |

17 | Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |

18 | Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |

19 | Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |

22 | Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with `preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |

34 | Schedules | Schedule views of rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, as Revit's Schedule/Quantities makes them: the fields chosen and ordered from the category's own (Area, Width, Count…), the project parameters for it and, for components, their families' parameters; calculated fields, formulas over the row's other fields as a family's are (`Area * 120`, `Perimeter * Finish Height / 1e6`); filters (equals, greater than, contains, begins with, has a value…) that every row holds to, comparing values as the schedule shows them; sorting by fields in turn, ascending or descending (the phase fields in the project's order of phases, not by name), and grouped, a row for each set of their values, its count and totals summed; totals under the rows. Every project has a Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedule, each the project's own once changed; CSV; on sheets, totals and all |

38 | Families | BIMCraft's own parametric components, never Autodesk's `.rfa`: a family has parameters (lengths, numbers, angles, yes or no, materials; each type's, or each component's), types that set them, and forms, each a profile drawn in its own axes and swept across them, every size a number or a formula as Revit's are (`Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`), each form of a material, there while a yes/no parameter or a formula says. A new project comes with ten of them (tables, chairs, beds, sofas, desks, wardrobes, base cabinets, WCs, washbasins, bathtubs), named and worded in its language; more load from .json files. A component places a family's type at a point, turned and mirrored, its instance parameters its own; plans show it from above, the parts under a higher one hidden (a table's legs under its top), and sections and elevations beyond their line, never cut, as Revit shows furniture; the 3D view shades each form in its material's colour, textured as its material is. A form may be turned about an axis in its plane (a pipe, a bowl, a shade: `axis`, and `from` and `to` in degrees, up to a full turn), and a `void` form cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through (a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, a sash round its pane), exactly: a solid cut by a solid, in any shape. The Family Editor in the desktop edits a family's parameters, types, forms and symbols as text, shows it on a preview you can turn, and makes it the project's, saves it to a `.json` file, or keeps it, with the materials it's made of, in the Favorites |

| `reload_cad` | | `cad` (a linked drawing's name): reads its file again, so every import of it shows what the file holds now |
| `cad_query` | | `id`, `at`, `reach?` (100 mm): the entity of an import nearest a point: its layer, kind, colour and linetype |

A `level` can be given by name or id; without one, commands use the lowest level. `render {view}` draws a plan (with
`ceiling: true`, its reflected ceiling plan), a section or an elevation by name, a sheet by number (a path ending .pdf prints it), or with `{3D}` (and `azimuth?`, `elevation?`) the 3D
view. `save` to a .pdf prints every sheet, a page each.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

content.content:
== door ['DR'] Door
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

== window ['WN'] Window
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

== rebar [] Rebar
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

== reinforce [] Reinforce
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes

== column ['CL'] Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

== structural_column ['CL'] Structural Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

== footing ['FI'] Isolated Footing
{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below

== beam ['BM'] Beam
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°

== strip_footing ['FW'] Wall Footing
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)

== pipe ['PI'] Pipe
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")

== duct ['DU'] Duct
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")

== conduit ['CN'] Conduit
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

== cable_tray ['CT'] Cable Tray
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep

== wire ['EW'] Wire
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

== down_conductor ['DC'] Down Conductor
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to

== ground_conductor ['GC'] Earthing Conductor
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)

== cabling ['CB'] Cabling
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

== stair [] Stair
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

== ramp [] Ramp
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

== railing [] Railing
{host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

== type [] Edit Type
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

== parameter [] Project Parameters
{name, kind?: text|number|length|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], rename?, delete?: true} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` (lengths in mm, yes or no as true or false). Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it. `inspect` lists them

== family [] Load Family
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

== component ['CM'] Component
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

== flip [] Flip
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

== modify [] Modify
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

== move ['MV'] Move
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves

== copy ['CO'] Copy
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

== rotate ['RO'] Rotate
{ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

== mirror ['MM', 'DM'] Mirror
{ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

== delete_type [] Delete Type
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family

== rename_type [] Rename Type
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type, name} renames a type of a category (`category` and `type`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`) to `name`, as Rename in Type Properties does: the elements of it, and what else names it, follow, and it keeps its GUID; refused for a name another type of it has. Text types and filled region types rename with `rename` on `text_type` and `filled_region_type`

== elements [] Elements
{category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

    id: Ref
    face: Face = "centre"
    point: Option<EndPoint> ?none
}

struct SegmentText {
    segment: usize
    prefix: String = "" ?empty
    suffix: String = "" ?empty
    above: String = "" ?empty
    below: String = "" ?empty
    replace: String = "" ?empty
}

struct Lock {
    segment: usize
    length: f64
}

struct Dimension @dimension {
    level: Ref
    view: Option<Ref> ?none
    kind: DimKind = "aligned"
    orient: Option<Orient> ?none
    refs: Vec<Reference>

    prefix: String = "" ?empty
    suffix: String = "" ?empty
    above: String = "" ?empty
    below: String = "" ?empty
    replace: String = "" ?empty

    equal: bool = false ?false

    edge: Option<[[f64;3];2]> ?none
}

struct Dimension3D {

    at: [f64;3]
    type: String = ""
}

struct Tag {
    host: Ref
    view: Option<Ref> ?none
    offset: P2
    leader: bool = false
    label: Option<String> ?none
}

struct Section {
    name: String

    end: P2

    graphics: Graphics = {} ?empty
}

struct Sheet {
    number: String
    name: String
    size: String
}

struct Viewport {
    sheet: Ref
    view: Ref
    at: P2
    scale: f64
}

struct Column {
    type: String
    level: Ref
    at: P2
    angle: f64 = 0.0
    top_level: Option<Ref>
    height: f64 = 0.0
    base_offset: f64 = 0.0

import math
cases = [
    ((0, 12000), (8000, 12000), 90, 2000, (1632.341034963229, 10862.472284718942)),
    ((0, 12000), (8000, 12000), 90, 6000, (5537.527843507288, 10556.103589299313)),
    ((20000, 0), (20000, 8000), -60, 3000, (19016.367202002442, 2815.5800315258784)),
    ((20000, 0), (20000, 8000), -60, 6000, (19132.359005293933, 5795.776383579374)),
]

def m1(a, b, arc, off):
    # centre from chord midpoint, radius = half chord / sin(half angle)
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(abs(t) / 2)
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    # distance from midpoint to centre
    h = r * math.cos(t / 2)
    # left normal
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    cx, cy = mx + nx * h * s, my + ny * h * s
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    ang = a0 + s * off / r
    return (cx + r * math.cos(ang), cy + r * math.sin(ang))

def m2(a, b, arc, off):
    # rotate the start vector about the centre
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / (2 * math.sin(t / 2))
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    h = (r * r - c * c / 4) ** 0.5
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    cx, cy = mx + nx * h * s, my + ny * h * s
    phi = off / abs(r) * s
    vx, vy = a[0] - cx, a[1] - cy
    co, si = math.cos(phi), math.sin(phi)
    return (cx + vx * co - vy * si, cy + vx * si + vy * co)

def m3(a, b, arc, off):
    # centre: tangent at start is chord rotated by -arc/2
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / (2 * math.sin(abs(t) / 2))
    cd = math.atan2(dy, dx)
    th = cd - t / 2  # start tangent direction
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    cx = a[0] - s * r * math.sin(th)
    cy = a[1] + s * r * math.cos(th)
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    ang = a0 + s * off / r
    return (cx + r * math.cos(ang), cy + r * math.sin(ang))

def m4(a, b, arc, off):
    # fraction of the sweep
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(abs(t) / 2)
    L = r * abs(t)
    f = off / L
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    h = r * math.cos(t / 2)
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    cx, cy = mx + nx * h * s, my + ny * h * s
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    ang = a0 + t * f
    return (cx + r * math.cos(ang), cy + r * math.sin(ang))

def m5(a, b, arc, off):
    # centre via sagitta: d = c/2 / tan(t/2) from midpoint along left normal
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    d = (c / 2) / math.tan(t / 2)
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    cx, cy = mx + nx * d, my + ny * d
    r = math.hypot(a[0] - cx, a[1] - cy)
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    ang = a0 + s * off / r
    return (cx + r * math.cos(ang), cy + r * math.sin(ang))

def m6(a, b, arc, off):
    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    d = (c / 2) / math.tan(t / 2)
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    cx, cy = mx + nx * d, my + ny * d
    r = math.hypot(a[0] - cx, a[1] - cy)
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    L = r * abs(t)
    ang = a0 + t * (off / L)
    return (cx + r * math.cos(ang), cy + r * math.sin(ang))

for name, f in [('m1', m1), ('m2', m2), ('m3', m3), ('m4', m4), ('m5', m5), ('m6', m6)]:
    res = []
    for a, b, arc, off, want in cases:
        got = f(a, b, arc, off)
        res.append('%s%s' % ('OK' if got == want else 'no', '' if got == want else ' %r vs %r' % (got, want)))
    print(name, res)

import json, math, subprocess, tempfile, shutil
Ds = [5, 10, 13, 20, 24, 25, 30, 36, 37, 47, 50, 60, 72, 90, 100, 133, 150, 180, 200, 250, 270, 300, 330, 359]
fams = []
info = []
for i, D in enumerate(Ds):
    frm = round(270 - D * 0.37, 3)
    to = round(frm + D, 3)
    name = 'R%d' % i
    fams.append('family ' + json.dumps({"name": name, "category": "generic", "parameters": [], "types": {"T": {}},
        "forms": [{"plane": "xy", "profile": [[1000, 0], [10000, 0], [10000, 100], [1000, 100]], "axis": [[0, 0], [0, 100]], "from": frm, "to": to}]}))
    info.append((name, D, frm, to))
cmds = []
for f in fams: cmds += ['--cmd', f]
for i, (name, D, frm, to) in enumerate(info):
    cmds += ['--cmd', 'component ' + json.dumps({"family": name, "at": [i * 1000, 0]})]
cmds += ['--cmd', 'elements {"category":"component"}']
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
p = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable', 'run'] + cmds, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
shutil.rmtree(d)
if p.stderr: print(p.stderr.decode())
v = json.loads(p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1])
hs = {e['family']: e['height'] for e in v['elements']}
for name, D, frm, to in info:
    h = hs[name]
    # z = -x sin(theta), x = 10000 max
    best = []
    for N in range(1, 200):
        zs = max(-10000 * math.sin(math.radians(frm + D * k / N)) for k in range(N + 1))
        zs = max(zs, 0)
        if round(zs, 2) == h:
            best.append(N)
    print(name, 'D', D, 'h', h, 'N candidates', best[:8])

import math, json, sys
from fractions import Fraction as F
def fma(a, b, c):
    return float(F(a) * F(b) + F(c))
proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outs = [json.loads(l) for l in open(sys.argv[2]) if '"category": "door"' in l or '"category": "window"' in l]
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in proj['elements'].values()}
def cands(s, e, o):
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    L = math.hypot(fx, fy)
    Ls = math.sqrt(fx * fx + fy * fy)
    Lf = math.sqrt(fma(fx, fx, fy * fy))
    Lf2 = math.sqrt(fma(fy, fy, fx * fx))
    r = {}
    for ln, LL in (('h', L), ('s', Ls), ('f', Lf), ('f2', Lf2)):
        ux = fx / LL; uy = fy / LL
        r['fma_u_' + ln] = (fma(ux, o, s[0]), fma(uy, o, s[1]))
        t = o / LL
        r['fma_t_' + ln] = (fma(fx, t, s[0]), fma(fy, t, s[1]))
        r['plain_u_' + ln] = (s[0] + ux * o, s[1] + uy * o)
        r['plain_t_' + ln] = (s[0] + fx * t, s[1] + fy * t)
        # lerp with fma: s + t*(e-s)
        r['lerp_' + ln] = (fma(t, fx, s[0]), fma(t, fy, s[1]))
        r['lerp2_' + ln] = (fma(t, e[0], fma(-t, s[0], s[0])), fma(t, e[1], fma(-t, s[1], s[1])))
    return r
score = {}
n = 0
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    if w.get('arc'):
        continue
    n += 1
    for k, v in cands(w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']).items():
        score[k] = score.get(k, 0) + (1 if v == tuple(o['at']) else 0)
print(n)
for k, v in sorted(score.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    print(k, v)

D2R = math.pi / 180.0
def cands(s, e, o):
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    L = math.hypot(fx, fy)
    r = {}
    th = math.atan2(fy, fx)
    r['ang'] = (s[0] + o * math.cos(th), s[1] + o * math.sin(th))
    r['ang2'] = (s[0] + math.cos(th) * o, s[1] + math.sin(th) * o)
    thd = th * R2D
    th2 = thd * D2R
    r['angdeg'] = (s[0] + o * math.cos(th2), s[1] + o * math.sin(th2))
    th3 = math.radians(math.degrees(th))
    r['angdeg_py'] = (s[0] + o * math.cos(th3), s[1] + o * math.sin(th3))
    # direction normalised then rotated by 0
    ux = fx / L; uy = fy / L
    r['u'] = (s[0] + ux * o, s[1] + uy * o)
    # centre-line offset with zero normal shift, computed as matrix
    r['mat'] = (s[0] + (ux * o - uy * 0.0), s[1] + (uy * o + ux * 0.0))
    # from the end
    r['end'] = (e[0] - ux * (L - o), e[1] - uy * (L - o))
    r['end2'] = (e[0] + ux * (o - L), e[1] + uy * (o - L))
    # mid
    mx = (s[0] + e[0]) / 2; my = (s[1] + e[1]) / 2
    r['mid'] = (mx + ux * (o - L / 2), my + uy * (o - L / 2))

    r['mid3'] = (mx2 + ux * (o - L / 2), my2 + uy * (o - L / 2))
    r['mid4'] = (mx + fx * ((o - L / 2) / L), my + fy * ((o - L / 2) / L))
    # sum of halves
    return r

    n += 1
    for k, v in cands(w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']).items():

import math, json, sys
proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outs = []
for f in sys.argv[2:]:
    outs += [json.loads(l) for l in open(f) if '"category": "door"' in l or '"category": "window"' in l]
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in proj['elements'].values()}
def xs(s, e, o):
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    L = math.hypot(fx, fy)
    Ls = math.sqrt(fx * fx + fy * fy)
    th = math.atan2(fy, fx)
    r = {}
    for nm, LL in (('h', L), ('s', Ls)):
        r['u*o/' + nm] = (s[0] + fx / LL * o, s[1] + fy / LL * o)
        r['d*(o/L)/' + nm] = (s[0] + fx * (o / LL), s[1] + fy * (o / LL))
        r['d*o/L/' + nm] = (s[0] + fx * o / LL, s[1] + fy * o / LL)
        r['o*d/L/' + nm] = (s[0] + o * fx / LL, s[1] + o * fy / LL)
        r['d*(1/L)*o/' + nm] = (s[0] + fx * (1 / LL) * o, s[1] + fy * (1 / LL) * o)
        r['lerp/' + nm] = (s[0] * (1 - o / LL) + e[0] * (o / LL), s[1] * (1 - o / LL) + e[1] * (o / LL))
        r['endback/' + nm] = (e[0] - fx / LL * (LL - o), e[1] - fy / LL * (LL - o))
    r['cos'] = (s[0] + o * math.cos(th), s[1] + o * math.sin(th))
    r['cos2'] = (s[0] + math.cos(th) * o, s[1] + math.sin(th) * o)
    return r
xsc = {}; ysc = {}
n = 0
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    if w.get('arc'):
        continue
    n += 1
    for k, v in xs(w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']).items():
        xsc[k] = xsc.get(k, 0) + (v[0] == o['at'][0])
        ysc[k] = ysc.get(k, 0) + (v[1] == o['at'][1])
print(n)
for k in xsc:
    print('%-16s x %d y %d' % (k, xsc[k], ysc[k]))

import math, json, sys
from fractions import Fraction as F
proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outs = []
for f in sys.argv[2:]:
    outs += [json.loads(l) for l in open(f) if '"category": "door"' in l or '"category": "window"' in l]
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in proj['elements'].values()}
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    s, e, off = w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    L = math.hypot(fx, fy)
    ux = fx / L
    want = o['at'][0]
    mine = s[0] + ux * off
    if mine != want:
        # exact real value of s.x + (true dx/L)*o
        sx, sy, ex, ey, oo = map(F, (s[0], s[1], e[0], e[1], off))
        dxe = ex - sx; dye = ey - sy
        Le2 = dxe * dxe + dye * dye
        import decimal
        decimal.getcontext().prec = 40
        Ld = decimal.Decimal(Le2.numerator) / decimal.Decimal(Le2.denominator)
        Ld = Ld.sqrt()
        uxd = decimal.Decimal(dxe.numerator) / decimal.Decimal(dxe.denominator) / Ld
        exact = decimal.Decimal(s[0]) + uxd * decimal.Decimal(off)
        print('want %r mine %r exact %s' % (want, mine, exact))
        print('   implied ux from want: %s ; fx/L = %r ; true ux %s' % ((decimal.Decimal(want) - decimal.Decimal(s[0])) / decimal.Decimal(off), ux, uxd))
        print('   ulps want-mine:', (want - mine) / math.ulp(want))

proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outs = []
for f in sys.argv[2:]:
    outs += [json.loads(l) for l in open(f) if '"category": "door"' in l or '"category": "window"' in l]
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in proj['elements'].values()}
def thetas(fx, fy):
    L = math.hypot(fx, fy)
    r = {}
    r['atan2'] = math.atan2(fy, fx)
    a = math.atan(fy / fx) if fx != 0 else math.copysign(math.pi / 2, fy)
    if fx < 0: a += math.pi if fy >= 0 else -math.pi
    r['atan'] = a
    r['acos'] = math.copysign(math.acos(fx / L), fy)
    b = math.asin(fy / L)
    if fx < 0: b = math.pi - b
    r['asin'] = b
    r['deg'] = math.radians(math.degrees(math.atan2(fy, fx)))
    r['deg2'] = (math.atan2(fy, fx) * (180 / math.pi)) * (math.pi / 180)
    return r
sc = {}
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    if w.get('arc'):
        continue
    s, e, off = w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    for k, th in thetas(fx, fy).items():
        x = s[0] + math.cos(th) * off; y = s[1] + math.sin(th) * off
        a = sc.setdefault(k, [0, 0])
        a[0] += (x == o['at'][0]); a[1] += (y == o['at'][1])
for k, v in sorted(sc.items(), key=lambda kv: -(kv[1][0] + kv[1][1])):

import math, json, sys
proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
outs = []
for f in sys.argv[2:]:
    outs += [json.loads(l) for l in open(f) if '"category": "door"' in l or '"category": "window"' in l]
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in proj['elements'].values()}
def cands(s, e, o):
    fx = e[0] - s[0]; fy = e[1] - s[1]
    r = {}
    for ln, L in (('hyp', math.hypot(fx, fy)), ('sq', math.sqrt(fx * fx + fy * fy))):
        inv = 1 / L
        r['(f*inv)*o ' + ln] = (s[0] + (fx * inv) * o, s[1] + (fy * inv) * o)
        r['f*(inv*o) ' + ln] = (s[0] + fx * (inv * o), s[1] + fy * (inv * o))
        r['f*(o*inv) ' + ln] = (s[0] + fx * (o * inv), s[1] + fy * (o * inv))
        r['(f*o)*inv ' + ln] = (s[0] + (fx * o) * inv, s[1] + (fy * o) * inv)
        r['f*(o/L) ' + ln] = (s[0] + fx * (o / L), s[1] + fy * (o / L))
        r['(f/L)*o ' + ln] = (s[0] + (fx / L) * o, s[1] + (fy / L) * o)
        # lerp forms
        t = o * inv
        r['s+(e-s)*t inv ' + ln] = (s[0] + (e[0] - s[0]) * t, s[1] + (e[1] - s[1]) * t)
        r['s*(1-t)+e*t inv ' + ln] = (s[0] * (1 - t) + e[0] * t, s[1] * (1 - t) + e[1] * t)
        t2 = o / L
        r['s*(1-t)+e*t ' + ln] = (s[0] * (1 - t2) + e[0] * t2, s[1] * (1 - t2) + e[1] * t2)
        r['e*t+s*(1-t) inv' + ln] = (e[0] * t + s[0] * (1 - t), e[1] * t + s[1] * (1 - t))
    return r
sc = {}
n = 0
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    if w.get('arc'):
        continue
    n += 1
    for k, (x, y) in cands(w['start'], w['end'], o['offset']).items():
        a = sc.setdefault(k, [0, 0])
        a[0] += (x == o['at'][0]); a[1] += (y == o['at'][1])
print(n)
for k, v in sorted(sc.items(), key=lambda kv: -(kv[1][0] + kv[1][1])):
    print('%-26s x %d y %d' % (k, v[0], v[1]))
